blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Accurate vegetation-encroachment assessment and risk mitigation require electric utilities to accurately locate and characterize distribution-network assets, including poles and power lines, and distinguish among medium-voltage, low-voltage, neutral, and telecommunication lines. Mobile and aerial Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds provide detailed 3D representations of these assets and their surroundings. However, power-line detection and reconstruction remain challenging because conductor returns are often sparse, incomplete, noisy, or occluded by vegetation. These challenges are especially significant in distribution networks, where lower pole heights and complex line configurations place conductors close to trees. In addition, mobile and aerial LiDAR datasets differ substantially in point density, viewing geometry, spatial coverage, and occlusion patterns. We propose a robust and automated reconstruction method combining scaled density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging to recover individual conductors under severe data incompleteness and occlusion. Following semantic classification, the same reconstruction pipeline processes both mobile and aerial LiDAR data without modality-specific code or parameter tuning. The method is evaluated through degradation experiments, benchmarking, parameter sensitivity analysis, and large-scale validation. On the aerial dataset, it achieves 96.87% precision, 96.66% recall, a 96.76% F$_1$-score, and a geometric RMSE of 0.127 m. On the mobile dataset, where conductor-level reference annotations were unavailable, it achieves a point-to-model RMSE of 0.045 m and a reconstruction coverage of 95.27%. Source code, documentation, and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/varen-project.

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
Reconstructing power-line geometry is essential for electric
utilities to assess vegetation encroachment and mitigate risks to
distribution infrastructure. Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point
clouds provide high-resolution 3D representations of utility assets and their surroundings, including vegetation, buildings, and roads [ 19 ] . Therefore, these data offer significant potential for automated power-network inspection, monitoring, and asset management. Nevertheless, reliable power-line detection and reconstruction from LiDAR point clouds remain challenging, particularly in distribution networks. Conductors and poles are often located close to trees and branches, resulting in frequent occlusions, sparse conductor returns, and confusion between power-line points and nearby vegetation.

blocks.en:
Traditional reconstruction methods, including voxel-based approaches [ 8 ] , often exhibit limited robustness to
incomplete or noisy point clouds and may incur substantial computational
costs on large datasets. More recent context-aware approaches [ 2 , 5 , 6 , 18 ] exploit pole locations, span geometry, and mathematical conductor models to estimate power-line shapes. Although they represent important advances, their performance may deteriorate under severe occlusion or substantial data incompleteness. Recent reviews have shown that many existing power-line extraction and reconstruction methods were evaluated on relatively small datasets and that comparatively few studies addressed complex multi-conductor configurations [ 16 ] . Furthermore, most have been evaluated on relatively limited datasets, leaving their robustness and scalability for large-scale power-network reconstruction insufficiently investigated.

blocks.en:
Existing methods are designed for a single LiDAR acquisition modality. Mobile LiDAR provides dense and detailed ground-level measurements, but its observations may be affected by
roadside obstacles, uneven sampling, and limited visibility of elevated
conductors. In contrast, aerial LiDAR provides broader spatial coverage
from a predominantly top-down perspective, but conductor returns may be sparser and more difficult to distinguish from nearby vegetation. These differences in point density, viewing geometry, spatial coverage, noise, and occlusion patterns complicate the development of a reconstruction method that performs consistently across both modalities. Consequently, a method developed for one modality may require substantial parameter retuning or implementation changes before being applied to the other.

blocks.en:
Recent learning-based studies have investigated power-line point extraction from both aerial and mobile LiDAR data [ 9 ] , unified conductor-level geometric reconstruction across these acquisition modalities remains insufficiently investigated. To the best of our knowledge, no previous power-line reconstruction
method has been specifically designed and extensively evaluated on both
mobile and aerial LiDAR data using the same reconstruction implementation and parameter configuration. Addressing this limitation is important for utilities that acquire heterogeneous LiDAR datasets and require a scalable solution without modality-specific reconstruction code or extensive manual calibration. Hence, we propose a robust and automated reconstruction framework that combines adaptive coordinate
prescaling, density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging to recover individual conductors under severe
occlusion and data incompleteness. The main contributions of this work
are as follows: 1. We develop a unified reconstruction framework for mobile and aerial LiDAR point clouds. Following modality-specific semantic classification, the framework uses the same reconstruction
implementation and parameter configuration for both acquisition
modalities. 2. We introduce a robust reconstruction method that combines
adaptive coordinate prescaling, HDBSCAN clustering, Huber-weighted polynomial fitting, iterative fragment merging, and a rescue stage for rejected conductor candidates. 3. We conduct an extensive evaluation that includes controlled degradation experiments, comparisons with existing reconstruction pipelines, and a comprehensive parameter-sensitivity analysis. The large-scale evaluation covers 1,620 mobile LiDAR spans over 68 km and 10,870 aerial LiDAR spans over 382 km. 4. We publicly release the source code, documentation, and
evaluation data. To the best of our knowledge, these resources
constitute the first publicly available benchmark that includes
power-line reconstruction data from both mobile and aerial LiDAR on https://github.com/varen-project .

blocks.en: II Related Work
blocks.zh: 二. 相关工作

blocks.en:
This section reviews representative methods for detecting, extracting,
and reconstructing power lines from LiDAR point clouds. Particular
attention is given to their assumptions, methodological strengths, and limitations regarding vegetation-induced occlusions, incomplete
conductor observations, closely spaced phases, and differences between
LiDAR acquisition modalities.

blocks.en:
Jwa et al. [ 8 ] introduced the Voxel-based Piece-wise Line
Detector (VPLD) for the automatic 3D reconstruction of power lines from airborne laser scanning (ALS) LiDAR data. Their method partitioned the point cloud into sub-cubic voxels and grouped neighboring voxels likely to contain conductor points. The resulting components were connected, and the parameters of a catenary model were iteratively refined to produce continuous conductor reconstructions. This piecewise strategy recovered
conductor geometry from locally detected observations, but its
performance deteriorated when conductor returns were sparse or heavily occluded by vegetation. Its voxel-based iterative processing could also incur substantial computational costs on large datasets.

Liang and Zhang [ 10 ] proposed a method for extracting power lines from ALS LiDAR data. Their method identified candidate conductor points through geometric filtering and applied a Hough-like line detector to organize and connect the extracted observations. The resulting points were modeled in 3D space using a
parabolic equation whose parameters were estimated by least-squares
fitting. However, the method became less effective under substantial
occlusion because large observation gaps prevented fragments belonging
to the same conductor from being correctly associated.

procedure [ 4 ] . By incorporating span-level contextual
information, their method reconstructed conductors even when portions of their LiDAR observations were missing. Nevertheless, it assumed that the conductor configuration remained sufficiently consistent throughout each span, which limited its applicability to spans containing
substantial horizontal or vertical configuration changes.

For mobile laser scanning (MLS) data, Gaha et al. [ 5 ] proposed a contextual method for detecting and
classifying utility poles and power lines. The search for conductor
candidates was restricted to points located near a plane defined by two
consecutive poles, thereby reducing the number of irrelevant observations and the processing complexity. RANSAC was used to extract approximately linear conductor segments, while RGB information was used to filter the resulting candidates. Subsequently, each conductor was modeled using three points, i.e., two points associated with consecutive poles and one point selected from the remaining candidates. The method was
evaluated on 98 poles and achieved a recall of 98% and an accuracy of
84%. However, the experiments were limited to single-phase configurations, and the three-point model was sensitive to candidate-point misclassification, particularly under severe occlusion. In a subsequent study, Massicotte et al. [ 13 ] extended
this approach by combining mobile LiDAR and image information to
support utility-asset inventory. The reported accuracy ranged from
85% to 95%.

Their method combined geometric feature extraction and clustering to identify power-line points and support hazard analysis. Although designed for dense ground-level observations, the method was not evaluated on aerial LiDAR data.

blocks.en:
More recently, Cao et al. [ 2 ] proposed an automated method for extracting power lines from ALS point clouds using connected-component segmentation and contextual geometric information. Their approach exploited the alignment of linear features with the span direction to distinguish conductor points from unrelated structures. To recover fragmented conductor segments, the authors introduced a graph-cut energy-minimization algorithm and a slice-based segmentation procedure that separated power lines from nearby pylons, insulators, and jumper wires. The method was evaluated on nine datasets covering more than 80 km of transmission corridors with voltage classes ranging from 220 to 800 kV. It achieved an average precision of 99.77%, an average recall of 99.81%, and an average F 1 -score of 99.79%. Despite its high reported performance, the method of Cao et
al. [ 2 ] relied on distance-based connectivity assumptions
that are unreliable when gaps within a conductor are larger than
the separation between neighboring conductors. This condition commonly
occurs in distribution networks, where phases are closely spaced, and
conductor observations may be fragmented by vegetation. Although these connectivity assumptions were suitable for transmission corridors with widely separated phases, they are less appropriate for dense
distribution-line configurations.

blocks.en: Maset and Fusiello [ 12 ] proposed a complete airborne-LiDAR processing pipeline combining deep-learning-based semantic segmentation, DBSCAN-based pylon identification, and J-Linkage multi-model fitting for conductor vectorization. The method achieved an F 1 -score of 98.5% for vectorized cables on a 36-km transmission-line dataset. However, it was evaluated on airborne high-voltage infrastructure and required explicit catenary-based multi-model fitting.

blocks.en:
The above studies demonstrated the value of combining contextual information with geometric conductor modeling. However, most methods are sensitive to severe occlusions, fragmented observations, or closely spaced conductors. When neighboring conductors are closely spaced, the extraction of individual conductors becomes challenging [ 17 ] . Generally, they were designed and evaluated for a single LiDAR acquisition modality.
Consequently, their robustness and scalability across mobile and aerial
LiDAR data remain insufficiently investigated. Table I summarizes the objectives, principal techniques, data sources, reported performance, and main
limitations of the reviewed methods. The reported values should be interpreted with caution because the studies used different datasets,
voltage classes, evaluation units, and metric definitions.

blocks.en:
The complete workflow consists of a modality-specific semantic
classification stage followed by a unified four-stage reconstruction
pipeline: 1) scaled clustering and geometric filtering, 2) robust
parametric conductor modeling, 3) iterative fragment merging and
conductor acceptance, and 4) rescue of rejected fragments. The semantic
classification procedure differs between mobile and aerial LiDAR data,
whereas all subsequent reconstruction stages use the same implementation and parameter configuration.

blocks.en: III-A Semantic Classification of Poles and Power Lines
blocks.zh: III-A 波兰语和电线语义分类

blocks.en: LiDAR semantic classification remains challenging because of variations in point density and intensity, occlusions, measurement noise, and scanning artifacts. Learning-based methods can address some of these limitations by jointly exploiting geometric, contextual, and RGB information.
blocks.zh: LiDAR语义分类仍然具有挑战性,因为点密度和强度、隐蔽性、测量噪声和扫描文物各不相同。 以学习为基础的方法可以通过共同利用几何、背景和RGB信息来解决其中一些局限性。

blocks.en:
For mobile LiDAR data, we trained a U-Next semantic-segmentation model [ 20 ] on an internally annotated dataset. A small
subset of point-cloud tiles was first manually annotated and used to train an initial model. The model was then applied to additional tiles, and its preliminary predictions were reviewed and corrected by a human annotator. The corrected annotations were incorporated into subsequent
training iterations. This model-assisted annotation procedure was
repeated until the classification performance stabilized. The final
model achieved an average Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 87%
over the critical power-line, vegetation, and pole classes. An example of the resulting semantic classification is shown in
Fig. 1 .

blocks.en: After HDBSCAN clustering using the implementation of McInnes et al. [ 15 ] , geometric and contextual criteria are used to remove likely classification errors. Clusters having a horizontal extent below 0.1 m are rejected. Also, PCA is applied to each cluster to assess its dominant orientation. Clusters whose principal direction is inconsistent with the span direction (absolute cosine below 0.85, i.e., a deviation larger than approximately 32 ∘ 32^{\circ} ) are considered unlikely to represent conductors and are removed. This filtering reduces vegetation points incorrectly assigned to the wire class. Fig. 2 shows the remaining clusters for the example in Fig. 1 .

blocks.en:
After clustering, observations belonging to a physical conductor can
remain divided among several spatially separated fragments, especially
when vegetation occluded parts of the conductor or when the LiDAR data
are sparse. A conductor model is therefore fitted to each cluster to identify geometrically compatible fragments. A catenary model can be fitted directly to the observed point coordinates without explicitly specifying the conductor’s physical properties such as conductor tension, temperature, and linear mass. We adopt a quadratic approximation for computational simplicity and stable fitting of highly fragmented observations. This choice is further supported by our experiments, in which quadratic fitting yielded slightly better reconstruction performance than catenary fitting. blocks.en: IV Experimental Evaluation

blocks.en: We evaluate the proposed method from four complementary perspectives: 1) controlled robustness to point thinning and occlusion, 2) large-scale performance on aerial and mobile LiDAR datasets, 3) comparison with existing reconstruction pipelines, and 4) sensitivity to the main algorithmic parameters.

blocks.en: IV-A Controlled Robustness Assessment
blocks.zh: IV-A 受控强力评估

blocks.en:
The controlled assessment evaluates the influence of data degradation on individual power-line spans. This assessment is challenging because spans differ in geometry, length, point density, and occlusion patterns, depending on the acquisition geometry and surrounding environment. To examine these effects under controlled conditions, we select three
representative span architectures from the mobile LiDAR dataset.
The mobile point clouds are acquired using a mapping unit equipped with two Velodyne VLP-32C LiDAR sensors, with a combined acquisition rate of two million points per second, an RTK-GPS system with a reported accuracy of ± 2 \pm 2 cm, and an inertial measurement unit. The point
clouds have an average density of approximately 1,200 points/m 2 and a reported positional accuracy of ± 3 \pm 3 cm. The data are preprocessed and divided into individual pole-to-pole spans containing the conductors located between two consecutive poles. Further details regarding span extraction are provided in [ 14 , 11 , 13 ] .
The selected architectures comprise: 1) a three-phase span,
2) a single-phase span, and 3) a horizontal-to-vertical span in which three horizontally arranged phases transition into a vertical
three-phase configuration. The third architecture represents a
complex case because the relative horizontal and vertical positions of the conductors vary along the span.

blocks.en:
The large-scale assessment evaluates the proposed method on
heterogeneous aerial and mobile LiDAR datasets. Since independent
conductor-level reference annotations are available only for the aerial dataset, the two modalities use different evaluation protocols. The aerial evaluation measures object-level detection and geometric reconstruction performance, whereas the mobile evaluation measures point-to-model geometric consistency and reconstruction coverage.

blocks.en:
The aerial dataset contains 10,870 pole-to-pole spans covering 382 km of distribution networks. It includes single-phase and
three-phase systems, mixed horizontal and vertical configurations, and both medium-voltage and low-voltage infrastructure. Individual span
lengths range from 4 to 160 m. The point clouds are acquired using a RIEGL VQ-1460 laser scanner
operating at a pulse repetition rate of up to 4.4 MHz. The point density ranges from 1 to 30 points/m 2 , and the reported vertical RMSE over
flat surfaces is 0.05 m. The LiDAR service provider supplies one 3D reference geometry for each physical conductor within each pole-to-pole span. The dataset contains 23,372 reference conductors. The reference geometries and predicted conductor models are expressed in the same coordinate reference system. Since the complete details of the provider’s proprietary annotation procedure are unavailable, we refer to these geometries as provider-supplied reference annotations rather than error-free ground truth.

We compare the proposed method with two existing reconstruction
pipelines using the controlled dataset described in

blocks.en: V Conclusion and Future Work
blocks.zh: 五. 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
This paper presents a robust method for reconstructing power-line geometry from sparse and occluded mobile and aerial LiDAR point clouds. Following semantic classification, the proposed pipeline applies the same reconstruction implementation and parameter configuration to both modalities. It combines span-aligned prescaling, HDBSCAN clustering, Huber-weighted polynomial fitting, iterative fragment merging, and a rescue stage for rejected fragments.
The controlled experiments demonstrate robustness to uniform point thinning, distributed gaps, and large contiguous occlusions. Under these conditions, the proposed method provides more consistent performance than the evaluated EPL and Cao-FEC pipelines. The sensitivity analysis
identifies the maximum fragment-merging distance as the most influential parameter, while showing relatively stable performance across the tested
HDBSCAN epsilon values. On 10,870 aerial spans containing 23,372
reference conductors, our method achieved a precision of 96.87%, a
recall of 96.66%, an F 1 -score of 96.76%, and a geometric RMSE of 0.12 m. On 1,620 mobile spans, it achieved a reconstruction coverage of 95.27% and a point-to-model RMSE of 0.045 m. The main limitations are the absence of independent conductor-level
annotations for the mobile dataset. However, the controlled robustness experiments and the aerial evaluation use independent conductor references and therefore partially mitigate this limitation. Another limitation is the reliance on generated semantic labels for aerial and mobile LiDAR, and the limited capability of the quadratic model to represent nonlinear, crossing, or intertwined conductors such as in Fig. 9 .
Future work will investigate orientation-aware hierarchical clustering and more flexible geometric models for these configurations. Moreover, it will strengthen the integration of conductor reconstruction with vegetation-encroachment assessment and utility decision-support tools [ 14 ] . To support reproducibility, we make the source code, documentation, and evaluation data publicly available at https://github.com/varen-project .
